Traces on von Neumann algebras

Written by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), September 2026. Self-checked by the writing AI. Original text: CC0 1.0.

A trace on a von Neumann algebra measures the size of positive elements, and it cannot tell x∗xx^*xx∗x from xx∗xx^*xx∗. The usual trace of matrices is the model. Since a trace gives equivalent projections the same value, it turns the comparison of projections into arithmetic. It is also the starting point of integration on von Neumann algebras.

This lesson develops traces from the definition up to the trace norm. We introduce the definition ideal of a trace and show that the usual forms of semifiniteness agree. For traces that take infinite values we construct supports, semifinite parts and sums. We prove that an algebra is finite exactly when its finite normal traces separate its positive elements. For a finite algebra we build the center-valued trace, and we show that every finite trace on it, normal or not, is determined by its values on the center. We extend normal traces from corners and amplify them by type I factors, and we show that an algebra is semifinite exactly when it carries a faithful semifinite normal trace. The last section introduces the trace norm and, for a faithful semifinite normal trace, identifies the completion of the definition ideal with the predual.

The lesson assumes the comparison theory of projections and the type decomposition, from Projections and types of von Neumann algebras; the basic structure of von Neumann algebras, from The double commutation theorem; and normal functionals and preduals, from The universal enveloping von Neumann algebra of a C*-algebra, and W*-algebras. One step uses Spatial tensor products of von Neumann algebras. The results used without proof are stated in full below.

Traces go back to the work of Murray and von Neumann on rings of operators (1936); the trace of a finite factor is constructed in [Murray–von Neumann 1937]. Other proofs that finite algebras carry traces came later, among them [Dixmier 1949] and [Yeadon 1971]; Section 4 uses Yeadon's fixed-point argument. Integration with respect to a trace goes back to Segal (1953) and [Dixmier 1953]; [Nelson 1974] presents Segal's theory through convergence in measure. Basic references are [Kostecki] and [Takesaki I].

Background used without proof

The following results are used as stated. In the proofs we refer to each of them by its name.

Comparison of projections. These facts are proved in Projections and types of von Neumann algebras.

MMM is the direct sum of its parts of type I, II1_11​, II∞_\infty∞​ and III, cut out by central projections zI,zII1,zII∞,zIIIz_{\rm I},z_{{\rm II}_1},z_{{\rm II}_\infty},z_{\rm III}zI​,zII1​​,zII∞​​,zIII​ with sum 111. Ideals and functionals.

  • σ\sigmaσ-weakly closed ideals. Every two-sided ideal of MMM that is closed in the σ\sigmaσ-weak topology equals MzMzMz for exactly one central projection zzz. This is proved in The double commutation theorem.
  • Normal functionals. A bounded linear functional on MMM lies in M∗M_*M∗​ exactly when it is completely additive on orthogonal families of projections. For a positive functional, preserving suprema of bounded increasing nets implies complete additivity, and membership in M∗M_*M∗​ implies preserving such suprema; so the two notions of normality agree. The first statement is proved in The universal enveloping von Neumann algebra of a C*-algebra, and W*-algebras.
  • Positive parts of normal functionals. A hermitian element of M∗M_*M∗​ is the difference of two elements of M∗+M_*^+M∗+​. Hence M∗M_*M∗​ is spanned by M∗+M_*^+M∗+​. This follows from the Jordan decomposition of a hermitian functional and the splitting of functionals into normal and singular parts, both proved in the same lesson.
  • Akemann's weak compactness criterion. Let K⊆M∗K\subseteq M_*K⊆M∗​ be bounded, and suppose that sup⁡ψ∈K∣ψ(pn)∣→0\sup_{\psi\in K}|\psi(p_n)|\to0supψ∈K​∣ψ(pn​)∣→0 for every decreasing sequence of projections pnp_npn​ with infimum 000. Then KKK is relatively σ(M∗,M)\sigma(M_*,M)σ(M∗​,M)-compact. Reference: [Akemann 1967].
  • Tensor products of isomorphisms. If π1:M1→N1\pi_1:M_1\to N_1π1​:M1​→N1​ and π2:M2→N2\pi_2:M_2\to N_2π2​:M2​→N2​ are ∗*∗-isomorphisms of von Neumann algebras, there is a ∗*∗-isomorphism of M1⊗ˉM2M_1\bar\otimes M_2M1​⊗ˉ​M2​ onto N1⊗ˉN2N_1\bar\otimes N_2N1​⊗ˉ​N2​ that sends x1⊗x2x_1\otimes x_2x1​⊗x2​ to π1(x1)⊗π2(x2)\pi_1(x_1)\otimes\pi_2(x_2)π1​(x1​)⊗π2​(x2​). This is proved in Spatial tensor products of von Neumann algebras; recall that a ∗*∗-isomorphism of von Neumann algebras and its inverse are normal.
  • The fixed point theorem of Ryll-Nardzewski. If QQQ is a nonempty weakly compact convex subset of a Banach space and GGG is a group of linear isometries of the space with g(Q)⊆Qg(Q)\subseteq Qg(Q)⊆Q for g∈Gg\in Gg∈G, then some point of QQQ is fixed by every g∈Gg\in Gg∈G. Reference: [Ryll-Nardzewski 1967]; a short proof is in [Namioka–Asplund 1967].

This section proves the facts about projections that the later sections use.

2. Traces and the definition ideal

Definition and first properties

Definition 2.1. A trace on MMM is a map τ:M+→[0,∞]\tau:M_+\to[0,\infty]τ:M+​→[0,∞] such that, for x,y∈M+x,y\in M_+x,y∈M+​, λ≥0\lambda\geq0λ≥0 and z∈Mz\in Mz∈M, τ(x+y)=τ(x)+τ(y),τ(λx)=λτ(x),τ(z∗z)=τ(zz∗).(2.1) \tau(x+y)=\tau(x)+\tau(y),\qquad \tau(\lambda x)=\lambda\tau(x),\qquad \tau(z^*z)=\tau(zz^*). \tag{2.1} τ(x+y)=τ(x)+τ(y),τ(λx)=λτ(x),τ(z∗z)=τ(zz∗).(2.1) It is faithful if τ(x)>0\tau(x)>0τ(x)>0 for every nonzero x∈M+x\in M_+x∈M+​; finite if τ(1)<∞\tau(1)<\inftyτ(1)<∞; semifinite if every nonzero x∈M+x\in M_+x∈M+​ majorizes a nonzero y∈M+y\in M_+y∈M+​ with τ(y)<∞\tau(y)<\inftyτ(y)<∞; and normal if τ(xi)↑τ(x)\tau(x_i)\uparrow\tau(x)τ(xi​)↑τ(x) whenever xi↑xx_i\uparrow xxi​↑x in M+M_+M+​.

A map M+→[0,∞]M_+\to[0,\infty]M+​→[0,∞] with the first two properties in (2.1) is called a weight. So a trace is a weight with the extra identity τ(z∗z)=τ(zz∗)\tau(z^*z)=\tau(zz^*)τ(z∗z)=τ(zz∗). For weights, semifiniteness can also be defined by density of the finite domain; Proposition 2.5 shows that for traces the two definitions agree.

Proposition 2.2. Let τ\tauτ be a trace on MMM.

  3. If e∼fe\sim fe∼f, then τ(e)=τ(f)\tau(e)=\tau(f)τ(e)=τ(f). If e≾fe\precsim fe≾f, then τ(e)≤τ(f)\tau(e)\leq\tau(f)τ(e)≤τ(f).

  6. (Finite traces.) Equivalent forms of semifiniteness

Proposition 2.5. For a trace τ\tauτ on MMM the following are equivalent. Normality is not needed.

  • (a) τ\tauτ is semifinite in the sense of Definition 2.1.
  • (b) Below each nonzero projection there is a nonzero projection of finite trace.
  • (c) There is an increasing net of projections eie_iei​ with τ(ei)<∞\tau(e_i)<\inftyτ(ei​)<∞ and ei↑1e_i\uparrow1ei​↑1.
  • (d) There is an increasing net of positive contractions ai∈Fτa_i\in F_\tauai​∈Fτ​ with ai↑1a_i\uparrow1ai​↑1.
  • (e) mτ\mathfrak m_\taumτ​ is σ\sigmaσ-weakly dense in MMM. This is the usual definition of semifiniteness for weights.

Proof. (a)⇒\Rightarrow⇒(b). Let e≠0e\neq0e=0 be a projection and 0≠y≤e0\neq y\leq e0=y≤e with τ(y)<∞\tau(y)<\inftyτ(y)<∞. Example 5.13 (Finite but not σ\sigmaσ-finite). Let Γ\GammaΓ be uncountable and M=ℓ∞(Γ)M=\ell^\infty(\Gamma)M=ℓ∞(Γ). It is finite, with T=idT=\mathrm{id}T=id. We prove a counting theorem and derive from it that this decomposition is unique.

Faithful semifinite normal traces on semifinite algebras

Theorem 6.7. For a von Neumann algebra MMM the following are equivalent:

  • (i) MMM is semifinite;
  • (ii) MMM has a faithful semifinite normal trace;
  • (ii′'′) MMM has a faithful semifinite trace (normality not required).

Proof. (ii)⇒\Rightarrow⇒(ii′'′) is trivial. (ii′'′)⇒\Rightarrow⇒(i): let τ\tauτ be faithful and semifinite. By Proposition 2.5(b), below each nonzero projection lies a nonzero projection of finite trace, and that projection is finite. So MMM is semifinite by Proposition 1.6(c).

(i)⇒\Rightarrow⇒(ii). Step 1: every nonzero central projection zzz majorizes the support of some nonzero semifinite normal trace. Exercise 2 (A projection of finite trace need not be finite). Let M=C⊕B(ℓ2(N))M=\mathbb C\oplus B(\ell^2(\mathbb N))M=C⊕B(ℓ2(N)) and τ(a⊕x)=a\tau(a\oplus x)=aτ(a⊕x)=a. The step "τ\tauτ restricted to eMeeMeeMe is a faithful finite trace, so eee is finite" needs faithfulness; here τ\tauτ vanishes on the infinite summand.

Exercise 5 (No center-valued trace on B(ℓ2)B(\ell^2)B(ℓ2)). Show that there is no linear map T:B(ℓ2(N))→CT:B(\ell^2(\mathbb N))\to\mathbb CT:B(ℓ2(N))→C with properties (a), (b), (c) of (5.2).

Solution. Property (b) is automatic, since the center is C1\mathbb C1C1. By (a), TTT is a positive linear functional with T(x∗x)=T(xx∗)T(x^*x)=T(xx^*)T(x∗x)=T(xx∗), that is, a finite trace, and T(1)=1T(1)=1T(1)=1 by (c). But B(ℓ2(N))B(\ell^2(\mathbb N))B(ℓ2(N)) is properly infinite, so Theorem 5.9(1) forces T=0T=0T=0, a contradiction. This does not conflict with Theorem 5.2, because B(ℓ2(N))B(\ell^2(\mathbb N))B(ℓ2(N)) is not finite.

Where this leads

  • The trace norm is the first step of integration with respect to a trace. The next steps are the duality between MMM and L1(M,τ)L^1(M,\tau)L1(M,τ), the Hilbert space L2(M,τ)L^2(M,\tau)L2(M,τ) with the standard representation of MMM on it, measurable operators, and the spaces Lp(M,τ)L^p(M,\tau)Lp(M,τ). Measurable operators and integration with respect to a trace are treated in the lesson Measurable operators and the integral for a trace.
  • For a finite algebra, T(x)T(x)T(x) lies even in the norm-closed convex hull of the unitary orbit of xxx. This is Dixmier's approximation theorem; Section 5 needs only the σ\sigmaσ-weakly closed hull.
  • A semifinite algebra has an extended center-valued trace, with values in the extended positive part of the center.
  • Many results above hold for traces that are not normal. Such traces, Dixmier traces for example, have a theory of their own.
  • Normal weights drop the identity τ(z∗z)=τ(zz∗)\tau(z^*z)=\tau(zz^*)τ(z∗z)=τ(zz∗). They are the subject of the course Modular Theory and Weights.
